topic.name: The Multivariable Chain Rule in Vector Form

question.text: Evaluate $\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t}[f(\mathbf r(t))]$ at $t=1$ given that $ \nabla f(x,y) = \dfrac {2x}{x^2+3y} \, \mathbf i + \dfrac{3}{x^2+3y} \, \mathbf j $ and $ \mathbf r (t) = t \, \mathbf i + t^2 \, \mathbf j. $
question.explanation:
The chain rule in vector form states that

\[ \dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t} [f(\mathbf r (t))] = \nabla f(\mathbf r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t). \]

In addition, we've been given that \[ \nabla f(x,y) = \dfrac {2x}{x^2+3y} \, \mathbf i + \dfrac{3}{x^2+3y} \, \mathbf j. \]

First, we substitute $x=t$ and $y=t^2$ into $\nabla f(x,y)$ to find $\nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)){:}$

\begin{align} \nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)) &= \dfrac {2(t)}{(t)^2+3(t^2)} \,\mathbf i + \dfrac{3}{(t)^2+3(t^2)} \,\mathbf j \\[3pt] &= \dfrac {2t}{t^2+3t^2} \,\mathbf i + \dfrac{3}{t^2+3t^2} \,\mathbf j \\[3pt] &= \dfrac {2t}{4t^2} \,\mathbf i + \dfrac{3}{4t^2} \,\mathbf j \\[3pt] &= \dfrac {1}{2t} \,\mathbf i + \dfrac{3}{4t^2} \,\mathbf j \end{align}

Now, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t),$ which is

\begin{align} \mathbf{r}'(t) &= \dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t}(t)\,\mathbf{i} + \dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t}(t^{2})\,\mathbf{j} \\[5pt] &= \mathbf{i} + 2t\,\mathbf{j} . \end{align}

Applying the chain rule, we get

\begin{align} \dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t} [f(\mathbf r (t))] &= \nabla f(\mathbf r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t) \\[5pt] &= \left( \dfrac {1}{2t} \,\mathbf i + \dfrac{3}{4t^2} \,\mathbf j \right) \cdot \left( \mathbf{i} + 2t\,\mathbf{j} \right) \\[5pt] &= \left( \dfrac {1}{2t}\right)\cdot1 + \left(\dfrac{3}{4t^2}\right)\cdot 2t \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2t} + \dfrac{3}{2t} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{4}{2t} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2}{t} . \end{align}

Finally, evaluating the above at $t=1,$ we obtain

\begin{align} \dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t} [f(\mathbf r (1))] &= \dfrac{2}{1} = 2. \end{align}

question.text: If $f(x,y) = 2x − xy^2$ and $\mathbf r (t) = \ln t \, \mathbf i +3t^2 \, \mathbf j,$ compute $\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t} [f(\mathbf r(t))].$
question.explanation:
The chain rule in vector form states that \[ \dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t} [f(\mathbf r (t))] = \nabla f(\mathbf r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t). \]

First, we need to compute $\nabla f(x,y){:}$ \begin{align} \nabla f(x,y) & = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} (2x - xy^2) \, \mathbf i + \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y} (2x - xy^2) \, \mathbf j \\[5pt] & = (2-y^2 ) \, \mathbf i - 2xy \, \mathbf j \end{align}

Next, we substitute $x = \ln{t}$ and $y = 3t^2$ into the above to find $\nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)){:}$ \begin{align} \nabla f(\mathbf r(t)) &= (2-9t^4) \, \mathbf i - 6t^2\ln t \, \mathbf j \end{align}

Now, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t),$ which is \begin{align} \mathbf r'(t) &= \dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t}(\ln t) \, \mathbf i + \dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t} (3t^2) \, \mathbf j \\[5pt] &= \dfrac 1 t\, \mathbf i +6t \, \mathbf j. \end{align}

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get \begin{align} \dfrac {\textrm d }{\textrm d t} [f(\mathbf r (t))] & = \nabla f(\mathbf r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t) \\[5pt] &= (( 2-9t^4) \, \mathbf i -6t^2\ln t \, \mathbf j) \cdot \left( \dfrac 1 t \, \mathbf i +6t \, \mathbf j\right)\\[5pt] &= (2-9t^4)\cdot\dfrac 1 t + (−6t^2\ln t)\cdot 6t \\[5pt] &= \dfrac 2 t -9t^3 −36t^3\ln t. \end{align}

question.text: If $f(x,y) = y\cos x$ and $\mathbf r (t) = \pi t \, \mathbf i + e^t \, \mathbf j,$ compute $\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t} [f(\mathbf r(t))].$
question.explanation:
The chain rule in vector form states that

\[ \dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t} [f(\mathbf r (t))] = \nabla f(\mathbf r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t). \]

First, we need to compute $\nabla f(x,y){:}$

\begin{align} \nabla f(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}(y\cos x) \,\mathbf{i} + \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}(y\cos x)\,\mathbf{j} \\[5pt] &= -y\sin x \,\mathbf{i} + \cos x\,\mathbf{j} \end{align}

Next, we substitute $x=\pi t$ and $y= e^t$ into the above to find $\nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)){:}$

\begin{align} \nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)) &= -e^t\sin \pi t \,\mathbf{i} + \cos \pi t \,\mathbf{j} \end{align}

Now, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t),$ which is

\begin{align} \mathbf{r}'(t) &= \dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t}(\pi t)\,\mathbf{i} + \dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t}( e^t)\,\mathbf{j} \\[5pt] &= \pi\,\mathbf{i} + e^t\,\mathbf{j}. \end{align}

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

\begin{align} \dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t} [f(\mathbf r (t))] &= \nabla f(\mathbf r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t) \\[3pt] &= \left( -e^t\sin \pi t \,\mathbf{i} + \cos \pi t \,\mathbf{j} \right) \cdot \left( \pi\,\mathbf{i} + e^t\,\mathbf{j} \right) \\[3pt] &= -\pi e^t\sin \pi t +e^t\cos \pi t \\[3pt] &= e^t (\cos \pi t - \pi\sin \pi t ) . \end{align}

question.text: If $f(x,y) = \ln \left(xy^2\right)$ and $\mathbf r (t) = t^{-2} \, \mathbf i + e^t \, \mathbf j,$ compute $\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t} [f(\mathbf r(t))].$
question.explanation:
The chain rule in vector form states that

\[ \dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t} [f(\mathbf r (t))] = \nabla f(\mathbf r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t). \]

First, we need to compute $\nabla f(x,y){:}$

\begin{align} \nabla f(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} \ln\left(xy^2\right) \,\mathbf{i} + \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y} \ln\left(xy^2\right)\,\mathbf{j} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{y^2}{xy^2} \,\mathbf{i} + \dfrac{2xy}{xy^2}\,\mathbf{j}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{x} \,\mathbf{i} + \dfrac{2}{y}\,\mathbf{j} \end{align}

Next, we substitute $x=t^{-2}$ and $y= e^t $ into the above to find $\nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)){:}$

\begin{align} \nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & = \dfrac{1}{t^{-2}}\,\mathbf{i} + \dfrac{2}{ e^{t}}\,\mathbf{j}\\[5pt] & = t^2 \,\mathbf{i} + 2e^{-t}\,\mathbf{j} \end{align}

Now, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t),$ which is

\begin{align} \mathbf{r}'(t) &= \dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t}(t^{-2} )\,\mathbf{i} + \dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t}( e^t )\,\mathbf{j} \\[5pt] &= -2t^{-3} \,\mathbf{i}+ e^t \,\mathbf{j}. \end{align}

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

\begin{align} \dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t} [f(\mathbf r (t))] &= \nabla f(\mathbf r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t) \\[3pt] &= \left( t^2 \,\mathbf{i} + 2e^{-t}\,\mathbf{j} \right) \cdot \left( -2t^{-3} \,\mathbf{i}+ e^t \,\mathbf{j}\right) \\[3pt] &=-2(t^2)(t^{-3}) + 2e^{-t}(e^{t})\\[3pt] &=2- \dfrac{2 }{ t } \\[3pt] & = \dfrac{2(t - 1)}{t}. \end{align}

question.text: Evaluate $\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t}[f(\mathbf r(t))]$ at $t=-1$ given that $\nabla f(x,y) =2x e^{x^2+y} \, \mathbf i +e^{x^2+y} \, \mathbf j$ and $\mathbf r (t) = \sin t \ \mathbf i + \left(t+\cos^2 t\right) \ \mathbf j.$
question.explanation:
The chain rule in vector form states that \[ \dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t} [f(\mathbf r (t))] = \nabla f(\mathbf r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t). \]

In addition, we've been given that \[ \nabla f(x,y) =2xe^{x^2+y} \, \mathbf i +e^{x^2+y} \, \mathbf j. \]

First, we substitute $x = \sin{t}$ and $y =t+ \cos^2{t}$ into $\nabla f(x,y)$ to find $\nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)){:}$ \begin{align} \nabla f(\mathbf r(t)) & = 2\sin t\, e^{\sin^2 t+t+\cos^2 t} \, \mathbf i +e^{\sin^2 t+t+\cos^2 t}\, \mathbf j \\[5pt] & = 2e^{t+1}\sin t \, \mathbf i + e^{t+1}\, \mathbf j \end{align}

Now, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t),$ which is \begin{align} \mathbf r'(t) &= \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d t} (\sin t) \, \mathbf i + \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d t}\left(t+\cos^2{t}\right) \, \mathbf j\\[5pt] & = \cos t \, \mathbf i + (1-2\sin t \cos t ) \, \mathbf j. \end{align}

Applying the chain rule, we get \begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d t} [f(\mathbf r (t))] & = \nabla f(\mathbf r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t) \\[5pt] & = \left( 2e^{t+1}\sin t \, \mathbf i + e^{t+1}\, \mathbf j\right) \cdot (\cos t \, \mathbf i + (1-2\sin t \cos t ) \, \mathbf j) \\[5pt] &= 2e^{t+1}\sin t \cdot \cos{t} + e^{t+1} \cdot (1-2\sin t \cos t) \\[5pt] &= 2e^{t+1}\sin{t} \cos{t}+e^{t+1} - 2e^{t+1}\sin{t} \cos{t}\\[5pt] &= e^{t+1}. \end{align*}

Finally, evaluating the above at $t = -1,$ we obtain \begin{align*} \dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t}\left [f\left(\mathbf r \left(-1\right)\right)\right] &= e^{-1+1}=1. \end{align*}
